Global warming = an increase in the average temperature of the earth’s atmosphere
Ecosystem – a natural community of plants, animals, and other organisms and the physical environment in which they live and interact.
Habitat – the place in the environment where a plant or animal lives.
Atmosphere – a mixture of gases, such as nitrogen, oxygen, and carbon dioxide, that surrounds t he Earth.

Weather – the current conditions of the atmosphere at a particular place and time. Some characteristics of weather are temperature, humidity, precipitation, cloudiness, wind, and atmospheric pressure. Weather conditions are temporary and change f requently
Precipitation – any moisture that falls to Earth, such as rain, snow, hail, sleet, or mist
Climate – the pattern of weather over a long period of time. Weather patterns for about 30 years can be used to describe the climate of a particular place .
Global Climate – the average climate of the entire Earth.
Climate Change – a significant change in the climate over time. Climate crisis

Greenhouse Gas – a natural or human -made gas that traps heat in the atmosphere. Examples of greenhouse gases include water vapor, carbon dioxide, methane, and ozone. Water Vapor, Carbon Dioxide , Methane
Ozone – a gas made up of three atoms of oxygen bonded together. Ozo ne high in the atmosphere protects the Earth’s surface from harmful ultraviolet radiation from the sun.
Ultraviolet Radiation – a type of invisible radiation that is released by the sun. Being exposed to ultraviolet radiation can cause sunburn and sometimes skin cancer and eye damage.

Global Warming –global warming occurs when there is “too much” of the greenhouse effect. Altho ugh the overall global temperature is warming, some places on the Earth may experience different climate changes. It takes an enormous amount of energy (heat) to change the climate of the whole planet.
Pollutant – a substance that contaminates the air or w ater. Pollutants can cause problems in ecosystems as well as health problems in humans.
Allergen – a substance that causes allergies. Examples include dust, mold, and pollen.

Infectious Disease – an illness caused by bacteria, viruses, parasites, or other organisms that enter and grow in the human body. Not all bacteria, viruses, and parasites that enter or live in the body cause disease. Some infectious diseases can be spread from person to person.

Such absorption with a virtual, rather than a physical, world has been blamed for an increase in unsociability and lack of co mmunication in young people. Such criticism has also been leveled at adults who similarly, spend hours on the internet. However, is such criticism just? Or is it unfounded? Obviously, using the internet purely as an information –finding tool or to play o n-line computer games, does not promote sociability and, hence, communication. In such instance the internet could rightly be argued to hinder the development and maintenance of social and communication skills. However, critics of the internet are overloo king its value as a powerful tool of communication, when used appropriately. On closer inspection, the internet could be argued to promote, rather than hinder, communication skills. Opponents of the internet and social networking sites argue though, that w ritten communications such as Twitter are inadequate substitutes for face -to-face contact. Whilst that may be true, Skype and video messaging have opened up a whole new world of communication. Admittedly, speaking to someone on screen is not a good substi tute for the real thing; however, it is a very workable alternative. If it were not, then video conferencing would not be the powerful tool of communication in the business world that it is today. So, used appropriately, the internet in my opinion is a hig hly effective tool of communication. Never before have we had the potential to communicate with so many people instantaneously on a global scale. It is not the internet itself that is destroying communication but its misuse
